title: Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means

content.overview: BNSS s. 105, Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means, is a procedural provision in the Processes to compel the production of things cluster. Apply its conditions in sequence, identify the competent criminal court and remedy, and check the s. 531 transition rule before using BNSS or the saved CrPC.

content.study:
Current-law identity
BNSS s. 105 governs recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means within Chapter VII - Processes to compel the production of things. The provision must be read with its enacted sub-sections, provisos, explanations, the BNSS First Schedule where classification or trial forum is relevant, and BNSS s. 104, BNSS s. 106.

Procedural meaning and legislative purpose
Criminal procedure is a sequence of safeguards, not a collection of isolated powers. This section allocates a procedural step to the police, Magistrate, trial court, Sessions Court or High Court and places conditions around its exercise. The mischief addressed is identified from the statutory text and Chapter setting; the court should not add a condition that the legislature did not enact or remove a safeguard that the text requires.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the proceeding, procedural stage and order sought.
2. Confirm whether the investigation, inquiry, trial, application or appeal was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. If so, begin with BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and test whether the saved CrPC route governs.
3. Quote the exact operative words of s. 105, including every condition, proviso and explanation.
4. Identify the competent criminal court, territorial rule, statutory sanction or classification requirement.
5. Map each material fact to the statutory condition it proves or fails.
6. State the immediate remedy and the standard for interference.

Evidence and constitutional control
The procedural record remains subject to Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The party asserting a factual foundation bears the ordinary burden under BSA s. 104; BSA s. 106 is limited to facts especially within a person's knowledge after the foundation is established. Electronic records must be separately tested under BSA s. 63 for the applicable certificate and production requirements. BSA admissibility does not cure an unlawful arrest, search, remand or other BNSS defect.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, state the current section first, identify the stage and forum, reproduce only the necessary statutory language, address the transition rule, apply each condition to the record, answer the principal objection, and request a precise order. Do not treat a police report as proof of guilt, an arrest as a conviction, a charge as a finding, or a procedural irregularity as automatically destroying the entire prosecution.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Doctrinal Foundation
sections.body:
BNSS s. 105 regulates recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means within Processes to compel the production of things.
Read the provision purposively but begin with its enacted text and the Chapter structure.
The constitutional background includes fair procedure, personal liberty and judicial accountability under Articles 14, 21 and 22.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos and Connected Provisions
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BNSS s. 105; do not replace the provision with a CrPC summary.
Read it with BNSS s. 104, BNSS s. 106. A connected section may define the condition, forum, time limit or remedy without replacing this section.
Use historical concordance only to explain development, never as the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Procedural Ingredients and Stage Test
sections.body:
First ingredient: the proceeding must be at the statutory stage addressed by s. 105.
Second ingredient: the competent officer or court must possess the relevant jurisdiction and power.
Third ingredient: each express condition, notice, reason, time limit, record or hearing requirement must be satisfied.
Fourth ingredient: the requested consequence must follow from the proved procedural breach or compliance; state the exact order sought.

sections.heading: BSA 2023 Burden and Electronic Evidence Checkpoints
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; do not shift the initial burden merely by invoking s. 106.
BSA s. 106 applies to a fact especially within knowledge only after the party relying on the legal proposition establishes the necessary foundation.
Where electronic material is tendered, separately examine relevance, authenticity, integrity, source and BSA s. 63 certificate requirements.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Transition
sections.body:
For proceedings under the post-1 July 2024 regime, cite BNSS s. 105 and verify the First Schedule or special statute where applicable.
For a matter pending immediately before commencement, apply BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and identify the saved CrPC procedure before addressing merits.
Check the applicable BNSS or special-statute limitation rule and calculate the remedy period from the actual order or event.

examples.title: Example 1 - Conditions satisfied
examples.body: A proceeding is at the stage governed by s. 105; the authorised officer or court records each statutory reason, follows the required notice and hearing path, and acts within jurisdiction. The order is tested against the section and its connected provisions.

examples.title: Example 2 - Boundary defect
examples.body: The decision-maker applies s. 105 without checking the procedural stage, the s. 531 savings rule or an express statutory condition. The advocate identifies the missing condition and seeks the precise procedural remedy rather than asserting an automatic result unsupported by the Act.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the order under BNSS s. 105 is sustainable and what immediate relief is available.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the stage and whether the proceeding was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. 2. State the exact test in s. 105. 3. Verify jurisdiction, notice, reasons, time limits and hearing requirements. 4. Test the electronic record separately under BSA s. 63. 5. Grant only the remedy supported by the proved defect, such as modification, release, disclosure, remand correction, quashing where maintainable or appellate interference.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: The petitioner sought registration of information disclosing a cognizable offence.
cases.issue: Whether registration is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Registration is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, subject to the limited preliminary-inquiry framework recognised by the Constitution Bench.
cases.holding: The Court directed compliance with mandatory registration and confined preliminary inquiry to recognised categories.
cases.relevance: Use only where s. 105 concerns information, investigation or a connected pre-cognizance step; do not treat this case as authority for every BNSS provision.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.facts: The case concerned arrest and detention for an offence carrying imprisonment up to seven years.
cases.issue: Whether arrest and remand may be authorised mechanically in a lower-punishment case.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police must satisfy and record the necessity conditions for arrest, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
cases.holding: The Court issued safeguards enforcing the discipline now reflected in the BNSS arrest framework.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 105 concerns arrest, custody, remand or liberty; otherwise identify a section-specific authority instead of forcing this case into the argument.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts: The Court addressed custodial violence and the absence of reliable arrest safeguards.
cases.issue: What minimum protections must accompany arrest and detention.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Arrest and custody require transparent documentation, accountability and safeguards protecting Articles 21 and 22.
cases.holding: The Court prescribed arrest and custody safeguards that inform the corresponding BNSS duties.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 105 directly engages arrest, custody, production or custody records; do not cite it as a substitute for the statutory text.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured legal brief on BNSS s. 105 - Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND JURISDICTION
Identify the procedural stage, competent forum, commencement status and precise order sought.

II. RULE
BNSS s. 105 governs recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means. Read its clauses, provisos and connected provisions BNSS s. 104, BNSS s. 106; then test s. 531 savings.

III. APPLICATION
Map each fact to jurisdiction, statutory condition, notice, reason, time limit and evidentiary foundation. Test electronic records under BSA s. 63 and burdens under ss. 104-106.

IV. CONCLUSION
State whether the order stands, must be modified or requires a specific procedural remedy.

learningObjectives: Master the statutory mandate under Section 105 BNSS requiring search and seizure procedures to be recorded through audio-video electronic means.
Understand the requirement to record the preparation of the seizure list (panchnama) and the signing by independent witnesses through electronic means.
Analyze the statutory duty of the police officer to forward the audio-video recording to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or Judicial Magistrate without delay.
Evaluate the evidentiary consequences under Section 63 BSA if the police fail to comply with the audio-video recording mandate.
enhancement.definition: BNSS s. 105 establishes the mandatory requirement of recording search and seizure through audio-video electronic means. It provides that the process of conducting search of a place or taking possession of any property, article or thing under this Chapter or under section 185, including preparation of the list of things seized and the signature of witnesses, shall be recorded through any audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone, and the police officer shall forward without delay such recording to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of first class.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Procedural transparency, elimination of planted recoveries, and digital integrity of physical evidence under Article 21. By mandating continuous electronic video documentation of searches and seizure lists, Section 105 prevents fabricated police recoveries and protects innocent citizens against evidence tampering.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VII — Processes to Compel the Production of Things, BNSS s. 105.
Scope of Application: Applies to all searches of places or seizure of property under Chapter VII and searches by police officers during investigation under Section 185 BNSS.
Mandatory Electronic Modality: Recording through audio-video electronic means, preferably by smartphone or digital body camera.
Panchnama Integration: The preparation of the seizure list and the signatures of independent panch witnesses must be captured in the recording.
Transmission Mandate: Mandatory obligation on the police officer to forward the digital recording without delay to the competent Magistrate.
essentialIngredients: The conduct of a search of a place or seizure of any property, article, or weapon under Chapter VII or Section 185 BNSS.
The continuous recording of the entire search and seizure process through audio-video electronic means.
The electronic documentation of the preparation of the seizure inventory list and the actual signing of the list by independent witnesses.
The prompt transmission of the digital recording (along with the seizure memo) without delay to the District Magistrate, SDM, or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.
examples: Teaching illustration (Compliant Narcotics Seizure): Police officers execute a search warrant at a suspect’s warehouse. Using a smartphone, a sub-inspector video-records the entire search, showing the recovery of 500 grams of contraband hidden under floorboards, the weighing and sealing in tamper-evident bags, the writing of the seizure memo, and two local shopkeepers signing the memo on camera. The video file is uploaded to the judicial magistrate’s portal the same evening with a Section 63 BSA certificate. The seizure is fully compliant with Section 105 BNSS.

Teaching illustration (Unrecorded Seizure / Vitiating Search): Police conduct a raid on a residential house and claim to have recovered an illegal firearm. They produce a paper memo but record no audio-video footage, despite possessing smartphones, and offer no explanation for the omission. The defence challenges the recovery under Section 105 BNSS. The trial court treats the unrecorded search with severe suspicion and disbelieves the recovery in the absence of electronic documentation.
distinctions: BNSS s. 105 vs CrPC 1973 s. 100: CrPC s. 100 required only paper search lists with two witnesses; BNSS s. 105 introduces mandatory audio-video recording of the search, the inventory preparation, and the witness signatures.

BNSS s. 105 vs BNSS s. 176(3): Section 105 mandates video recording of search and seizure of property; Section 176(3) mandates forensic expert crime scene inspection and video recording of the entire crime scene for heinous offences carrying 7+ years.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether physical articles seized during a nighttime house search under Section 185 BNSS are admissible in evidence when the police officer deliberately failed to record the search on audio-video electronic means.

Rule: Under Section 105 BNSS, the recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means is a mandatory statutory command designed to ensure integrity; unexplained non-compliance creates a serious procedural defect.
Application: The police officers had working mobile phones but deliberately switched them off during the search, offering no technical justification for the failure to record.

Conclusion: The deliberate violation of Section 105 BNSS severely impairs the credibility of the seizure; the court must draw an adverse inference against the prosecution regarding the authenticity of the recovery.

shortAnswer: State the statutory mandate of Section 105 BNSS (mandatory audio-video recording of search and seizure).
Explain that recording must capture the inventory preparation and witness signatures.
State the duty to forward the recording without delay to the Magistrate.

Scope of application: Searches under Chapter VII and investigative searches under Section 185.

sixteenMark: Constitutional due process: Article 21, the right to privacy, and protection against arbitrary police searches.
Historical critique of Section 100 CrPC: Hostile panch witnesses and the problem of planted evidence.
Exhaustive textual analysis of BNSS Section 105: Modality (smartphones/body cameras), panchnama recording, and prompt judicial submission.
Interlock with the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: Evidentiary admissibility of search videos under Section 63 and hash value integrity.
Judicial remedies: Quashing of illegal searches, adverse inferences, and disciplinary liability for non-compliance.

Critical assessment of digital infrastructure preparedness in police stations across India.

keyTakeaways: BNSS s. 105 mandates audio-video electronic recording for all searches and seizures of property.
The recording must encompass the entire search process, the drafting of the inventory list, and the signing by witnesses.
Recordings must be forwarded without delay to the competent Judicial or Executive Magistrate.
Forms a critical digital safeguard alongside Section 63 BSA to ensure the authenticity of recoveries.
